title: Elder abuse and Adult Protective Services in New York
seoTitle: Report Elder Abuse in New York: APS, Scams, Who to Call
seoDesc: How to report elder abuse, neglect or money exploitation in New York: NYC and county Adult Protective Services, scam hotlines, the ombudsman and what APS does.
dek: If you think an older New Yorker is being hurt, neglected or cheated, you can make a report today. Here is who to call in New York City and the rest of the state, and what happens next.
keyFacts: Danger right now: call 911
NYC Adult Protective Services: 718-557-1399, weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., or 311
Statewide APS helpline: 1-844-697-3505, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.
APS serves adults 18+ regardless of income; NYC accepts anonymous reports
Scams: NY Attorney General helpline 1-800-771-7755
body:
If an older adult is in danger right now, call 911. For abuse, neglect or money being taken that is not an emergency, call Adult Protective Services (APS). In New York City, that is 718-557-1399. Everywhere else, it is your county Department of Social Services, or the state APS helpline at 1-844-697-3505.

You do not need proof to make a report. You only need a real concern. This guide explains who APS helps and what happens after you call. It also covers money abuse, scams and problems in nursing homes or assisted living.

Who do I call about elder abuse in New York?

SituationWho to call
Someone is in immediate danger911
Abuse, neglect or self-neglect in the five boroughsNYC APS at 718-557-1399, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., or 311. Online at nyc.gov/apsrefer
Abuse, neglect or self-neglect elsewhere in the stateYour county Department of Social Services APS unit, or the NYS APS helpline at 1-844-697-3505, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Not sure if it is abuse and want to talk it throughElder Abuse Helpline for Concerned Persons, 844-746-6905
Domestic violence, including by a spouse or partnerNYS Domestic and Sexual Violence Hotline, 1-800-942-6906 (711 for deaf and hard of hearing callers), 24 hours
Scams and consumer fraudNY Attorney General, 1-800-771-7755
Problems in a nursing home, adult home or assisted livingLong Term Care Ombudsman Program, 1-855-582-6769

Outside the city, county APS units have their own local numbers. You can find yours through the state Office of Children and Family Services or by calling the state APS helpline above.

Who does Adult Protective Services help?

APS helps adults 18 and older, at any income level, who meet all three of these conditions.

  • They have a physical or mental impairment.
  • Because of it, they cannot manage their money, meet their daily needs or protect themselves from abuse, neglect, exploitation or other hazards without help.
  • They have no one available who is willing and able to help them responsibly.

That last point matters. If your father has a capable daughter helping, APS may decide he does not need its services. If the person hurting him is the one "helping," that person does not count.

APS also handles self-neglect. That might be an older neighbor in Yonkers who has stopped eating, is surrounded by spoiled food and will not let anyone in.

You do not need proof to call. A real worry is enough.

What happens after I make a report?

  1. Intake. A worker asks what you have seen and how to reach the person. NYC APS accepts anonymous referrals and keeps the information confidential.
  2. Screening. APS decides whether the person appears to meet the three conditions above.
  3. Home visit. In NYC, APS visits within 24 hours if the situation looks life threatening, and within three business days in other cases.
  4. Decision. After the visit, APS decides whether to open a case. Some counties, such as Tompkins, tell the person who made the report whether the case was accepted.
  5. Service plan. If the case is opened, a caseworker builds a plan with the person and checks in over time.

Can my parent say no?

Often, yes. Adults have the right to make their own choices, including choices their family disagrees with. If the person refuses help and is judged safe with the supports they have, the case may close. If the situation is unsafe, APS keeps the case open and keeps trying to engage them. Tompkins County APS explains that it cannot force treatment for mental health or substance use, unless there is an immediate danger to the person or others.

When someone truly cannot make decisions, a court may need to appoint a guardian. See our Article 81 guardianship guide.

What can APS actually do?

New York City's APS brochure lists the kinds of help a caseworker can arrange, depending on the plan.

  • Medical and psychiatric exams and ongoing care
  • Help applying for or renewing Medicaid and home care
  • Help with rent and utility arrears
  • Public assistance, SSI and SSD benefits
  • Housing Court help to prevent eviction
  • Other living arrangements
  • Managing Social Security benefits for someone who cannot
  • Referrals to the NYPD and the District Attorney for abuse or exploitation
  • Heavy-duty cleaning
  • Court petitions for a community guardian to manage financial and household affairs

Counties outside the city offer similar case management, but the details vary. Ask your county APS what it can provide.

What does financial exploitation look like?

Money abuse is often quiet. It can come from a stranger, a new "friend," a paid helper or a relative. The Department of Financial Services (DFS) lists these warning signs.

  • Unpaid bills the person should be able to pay
  • Sudden or unexplained transfers of money or property
  • Confusion about recent financial changes
  • Unusual spending
  • A new close acquaintance who seems to want access to accounts
  • Recent changes to a will, trust or insurance policy

What to do

  • Call APS if the person seems unable to protect themselves.
  • Call DFS at 1-800-342-3736. DFS says it can take complaints and investigate suspected elder financial exploitation.
  • Call local police if money was stolen.
  • Call the bank's fraud department and ask about freezing or flagging the account.

A durable power of attorney with an agent your parent trusts can prevent a lot of this. See our power of attorney guide.

Which scams target older New Yorkers?

The state Office for the Aging cites FBI figures showing adults over 60 lost more than $3.4 billion to scams in 2023. The NY Attorney General and the state Office for the Aging warn about these common ones.

  • Grandparent scam. A caller pretends to be a grandchild in trouble and begs for money, often asking you not to tell the parents.
  • Government imposters. Callers claim to be from the IRS, Medicare or Social Security. The state Office for the Aging says no federal agency will call you out of the blue like this.
  • Gift card requests. Anyone who asks you to pay with gift cards and read the numbers over the phone is running a scam.
  • Prize and sweepstakes scams. Real contests never ask for money up front.
  • Fake checks. You deposit a check, wire some back, and the check bounces later.
  • Home repair scams. Someone knocks with leftover material from a job "around the corner," or a "free inspection" finds costly problems.
  • Tech support scams. A pop-up says the computer is infected and gives a number to call. Never let a stranger take remote control.
  • Romance scams. A new online love interest who needs money.
  • Parcel and phishing texts. Messages about a missed delivery or a locked account that ask for personal details.

Where to report a scam

  • NY Attorney General helpline: 1-800-771-7755 (deaf or hard of hearing: 1-800-788-9898), or online at ag.ny.gov/file-complaint
  • Federal Trade Commission: reportfraud.ftc.gov
  • FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center: ic3.gov
  • Local police, using 911 to file a report
A simple family rule

Agree that no one in the family sends money because of a call, text or email without first hanging up and calling back on a number you already know. The Attorney General advises hanging up and contacting the company yourself.

Who helps people in nursing homes and assisted living?

The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program advocates for residents of nursing homes, assisted living and other licensed adult care homes. Ombudsmen help resolve complaints, explain residents' rights and work with residents, families and staff. When a problem cannot be fixed that way, they can refer it to the state Department of Health or another agency.

Call 1-855-582-6769 or use the Find Your Ombudsman page. If you suspect abuse that puts a resident in danger, call 911 first. Checking a home's record before a move also helps. See our nursing home ratings guide.

What other help is there in New York City and upstate?

  • NYC Aging Elder Justice programs. Community partners in each borough offer case help, crisis intervention, safety planning, shelter referrals, counseling and help with Family, Criminal and Housing courts. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.
  • NYC Aging C-PASS. The Crime Prevention and Support Services program helps older adults hit by scams, theft, robbery, harassment or assault. It can help file complaints with the FTC or FBI and apply to the state Office of Victim Services for crime-related losses.
  • Upstate Elder Abuse Center at Lifespan. Call 1-866-454-5110.
  • NY Connects. For services that can lower risk, such as home care, meals and caregiver support, call 1-800-342-9871. See our caregiver support guide.

How to stay calm and helpful

  • Write down what you saw, with dates. Keep copies of odd bank statements or letters.
  • Talk to your parent alone, in a quiet moment. Ask open questions and listen.
  • Do not confront a suspected abuser in a way that could put your parent at more risk.
  • Make the report, then keep visiting and calling. Staying close helps protect your parent.

faq.q: How do I report that my mom is being taken advantage of in the Bronx?
faq.a: Call NYC Adult Protective Services at 718-557-1399, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., call 311, or refer online at nyc.gov/apsrefer. If money was stolen, also call the police. If she is in danger right now, call 911.

faq.q: Who do I call about my dad being neglected by a caregiver in Syracuse?
faq.a: Call Onondaga County's Adult Protective Services unit, or the state APS helpline at 1-844-697-3505, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. If he is in immediate danger, call 911.

faq.q: Can I report elder abuse anonymously in New York?
faq.a: Yes. New York City APS accepts anonymous referrals and keeps the information confidential. Outside the city, county APS units such as Tompkins County's keep the caller's identity confidential unless you want the person to know.

faq.q: Does Adult Protective Services cost money or have an income limit?
faq.a: APS serves adults 18 and older regardless of income. Eligibility depends on having an impairment, being unable to protect themselves or manage daily needs, and having no one willing and able to help.

faq.q: Can APS remove my parent from their home?
faq.a: APS works to help people stay safely at home and adults can usually refuse services. If someone cannot make decisions and is at risk, a court may appoint a guardian, which is a separate legal process.

faq.q: Where do I report a scam call targeting an older adult in New York?
faq.a: Call the NY Attorney General's helpline at 1-800-771-7755 or file online at ag.ny.gov/file-complaint. You can also report to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov and to the FBI at ic3.gov.

title: Help for family caregivers in New York: respite, leave and support
seoTitle: Help for Family Caregivers in New York (2026 Guide)
seoDesc: Where New York family caregivers get help: county Offices for the Aging, NYC Aging, respite, dementia support, Paid Family Leave figures and tax credits.
dek: New York has free counseling, respite, dementia support and paid leave for people caring for an older relative. Here is where to start, who qualifies and what each program pays.
keyFacts: Start with NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 in NYC
Family caregiver support covers adults caring for someone 60+, or anyone with dementia
NY Paid Family Leave pays 67% of your average weekly wage for up to 12 weeks
PFL weekly maximum is $1,228.53 in 2026 and $1,287.91 for leave starting in 2027
NY's child and dependent care credit can cover care for a disabled spouse or adult dependent
body:
If you are helping a parent or spouse with bills, meals, rides or personal care, New York has help for you. Your first call is NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 if your loved one lives in one of the five boroughs.

The state says 4.1 million New Yorkers take on a caregiving role each year, giving more than 2.6 billion hours of hands-on care. Many of them never call it caregiving. This guide covers the free support programs, respite, dementia help, Paid Family Leave and the tax credits that can ease the cost.

Where does a family caregiver in New York start?

Caregiver help in New York runs through the local Area Agency on Aging. Outside New York City, that is your county Office for the Aging (some counties use a slightly different name). Inside the city, it is NYC Aging, the city's Department for the Aging.

  • Outside NYC: Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. It routes you to the county where your loved one lives, which matters more than where you live.
  • In the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens or Staten Island: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC), Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.

You do not need to live with the person you care for. New York's Caregiver Resource Centers serve family members and other informal caregivers whether or not they live together. That helps if you live in Albany and your dad lives in Binghamton.

Call the county where your parent lives, even if you live somewhere else.

The state also runs a free online Caregiver Portal at newyork-caregivers.com, with free resources and training for unpaid caregivers. Read more about the front door to services in our guide to NY Connects.

What does the National Family Caregiver Support Program offer?

The National Family Caregiver Support Program (NFCSP) is a federal program under the Older Americans Act. In New York, county Offices for the Aging and NYC Aging run it. It pays for services aimed at the caregiver, so you are the client.

Who can get NFCSP helpDetails
Caregiver of an older adultAdult relative or other unpaid caregiver of someone 60 or older
Dementia caregiverAdult caregiver of someone of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder
Grandparents and other relatives raising childrenNon-parent relatives 55 or older raising a child under 18
Older parents of adults with disabilitiesRelatives 55 or older, including parents, caring for an adult 18 to 59 with a disability

The program offers five kinds of help.

  • Information about services near you.
  • Help getting connected, including applying for benefits.
  • Counseling, support groups and training, so you can make care decisions and solve problems with less guesswork.
  • Respite, meaning short breaks while someone else provides care.
  • Supplemental services on a limited basis. In New York these can include home-delivered meals, personal emergency response buttons, minor home changes, assistive devices and legal services.

Funding is limited and every county sets its own mix. Ask what is available now, how long the wait is and if there is a suggested contribution.

What help is there for caregivers in New York City?

NYC Aging estimates there are 1.3 million family caregivers in the city. Its caregiver programs work through community partners in every borough. They offer:

  • Information, referrals and long-term care planning
  • Support groups and one-on-one counseling
  • Caregiver training
  • Respite care
  • Help applying for benefits
  • Limited financial assistance

Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and say you are a caregiver. They will match you with the caregiver program that covers your loved one's community district. The NYC Aging caregiving page also has a Service Finder to locate programs near you.

NYC Aging funds some social adult day programs too. These give your parent supervision, meals and activities during the day, and give you predictable time off. Most centers are private and are paid by Medicaid or by the family, so ask about cost before you visit.

How do I get a break from caregiving?

Respite is short-term care so you can rest, work, see a doctor yourself or travel. It can be a few hours of in-home help, a day program or an overnight stay. A planned break is easier to arrange than an emergency one, so ask early.

Here are the main routes to respite in New York.

  • NFCSP respite through the county Office for the Aging or NYC Aging, for the caregivers listed above. In NYC this can include in-home day or night care, adult day services or an overnight stay in a nursing home.
  • EISEP respite. The state's in-home program for people 60+ who are not on Medicaid includes respite for family caregivers outside of a nursing home or other facility. See our EISEP guide.
  • Dementia respite through the state's regional Alzheimer's caregiver programs (see below).
  • Medicaid home care. If your parent has Medicaid, home care hours may let you step back. Some families use the consumer directed program so a relative can be paid as the aide. See our CDPAP guide and Medicaid guide.

Questions to ask when you call

  • Is there a waiting list for respite, and how long is it?
  • How many hours could we get, and how often?
  • Is there a cost share or a suggested contribution?
  • Can respite happen at home, or only at a day program or facility?
  • Do you have support groups at times I can attend, in person or by video?

What help is there for dementia caregivers?

The New York State Department of Health funds three statewide Alzheimer's programs. It calls this a $25 million annual investment in community support and health services.

ProgramWhat it offers
Alzheimer's Disease Regional Caregiver Support InitiativeTen regional organizations offering caregiver assessments, support groups, education, wellness programs and respite care
Alzheimer's Disease Community Assistance ProgramRun by Alzheimer's Association chapters, with a 24-hour helpline at 800-272-3900 for information and referrals
Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's DiseaseTen regional centers that diagnose and manage dementia and refer families to community support

To find the providers for your parent's county, use the Health Department's county program list. In New York City, NYC Aging's caregiver programs also serve caregivers of people of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder.

If you are early in the dementia journey, a Center of Excellence visit can confirm the diagnosis and give you a plan. It is also a good time to sign a health care proxy and a power of attorney while your parent can still do so.

Can I get paid leave from work to care for a parent?

Yes, if you work for a private employer in New York. New York Paid Family Leave (PFL) gives job-protected, paid time off to care for a family member with a serious health condition. Workers pay for it through a small payroll deduction.

Paid Family Leave2026Leave starting in 2027
Benefit67% of your average weekly wage, up to the cap
Maximum weekly benefit$1,228.53$1,287.91
NY State Average Weekly Wage$1,833.63$1,922.25
LengthUp to 12 weeks
Employee contribution0.432% of gross wages, up to $411.91 a year0.452% of gross wages, up to $451.81 a year

The state puts the maximum total benefit for leave starting in 2027 at $15,454.92, which is 12 weeks at the top weekly rate.

Who counts as family?

You can take PFL to care for a spouse, domestic partner, child or stepchild, parent or stepparent, parent-in-law, grandparent, grandchild or sibling. The family member can live outside New York. So a daughter in Rochester can take leave to help her mother after surgery in Florida.

Am I eligible?

  • If you work 20 or more hours a week, you qualify after 26 consecutive weeks with your employer.
  • If you work under 20 hours a week, you qualify after 175 days worked, which do not need to be in a row.
  • Citizenship and immigration status do not affect eligibility.

You can take leave all at once or in full-day pieces. Someone who works three days a week, for example, can take up to 36 separate days.

How to apply

  1. Tell your employer. Give at least 30 days' notice if the leave is foreseeable, or as soon as you can if it is not.
  2. Get the forms. You need the Request for Paid Family Leave (PFL-1) and the Health Care Provider Certification (PFL-4). Your parent signs a release (PFL-3) and gives it to their doctor. The PFL-3 does not go to the insurer.
  3. Fill in your parts. Give the PFL-1 to your employer, who must return it within three business days. Have your parent's doctor complete their part of the PFL-4.
  4. Send everything to your employer's insurance carrier. Mail or fax the forms within 30 days after your leave begins.
  5. Call the helpline if you get stuck. The PFL Helpline is 844-337-6303, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

If you work for a government employer, ask human resources if you are covered. The full rules are at paidfamilyleave.ny.gov.

What tax help is there for caregivers in New York?

New York has no general tax credit just for being a family caregiver. Two state credits can still help, depending on your situation.

  • Child and dependent care credit. It is not only for children. It can cover care for a disabled spouse who cannot care for themselves. It can also cover another disabled person who cannot care for themselves, lived with you more than half the year and is your dependent. You must qualify for the federal credit first. For full-year residents, the state credit is fully refundable. The separate New York City credit only covers care for a child under 4, so it does not apply to care for a parent or spouse. See the Tax Department's credit page.
  • Long-term care insurance credit. If you pay premiums on a qualifying long-term care policy, the state gives a nonrefundable credit of 20% of the premiums paid that year. For individuals, it is capped at $1,500 and is limited to people with New York adjusted gross income under $250,000. It is claimed on Form IT-249. See the credit page.

Federal rules on claiming a parent as a dependent and deducting medical costs are separate. A tax preparer, or a free volunteer tax site, can check what fits your family.

What mistakes do new caregivers make?

  • Waiting for a crisis. Many programs have waiting lists. Call after the first fall or the first scary forgetful moment, before a hospital stay forces your hand.
  • Calling the wrong county. Services follow the person receiving care. Call the office where your parent lives.
  • Skipping the legal papers. Without a health care proxy and power of attorney, you may face a court case later. See our guardianship guide for what that involves.
  • Not telling your employer. PFL has a notice rule and a 30-day window to file. Missing either can delay your pay.
  • Doing it all alone. More than half of unpaid caregivers in New York do not see themselves as caregivers, according to the state. Saying the word out loud on the phone opens doors.
After a hospital stay

Ask the hospital discharge planner for a referral to your county Office for the Aging or NYC Aging before your parent leaves. A case manager can start the paperwork for home care, meals and respite while you focus on the trip home.

faq.q: How do I get help caring for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and say you are a family caregiver. NYC Aging will connect you with the caregiver program for your mom's community district, which can offer counseling, support groups, training, respite and benefits help.

faq.q: Can I get paid to take time off to care for my dad in Buffalo?
faq.a: If you work for a private employer in New York, Paid Family Leave can pay you 67% of your average weekly wage for up to 12 weeks. The cap is $1,228.53 a week in 2026 and $1,287.91 for leave starting in 2027. Your dad can live anywhere, including out of state.

faq.q: Who runs caregiver support outside New York City?
faq.a: Each county Office for the Aging runs the National Family Caregiver Support Program and other services. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to reach the office in the county where your loved one lives.

faq.q: Is there help for caregivers of someone with dementia in New York?
faq.a: Yes. The state Health Department funds regional caregiver support programs with assessments, support groups, education and respite. There is also a 24-hour Alzheimer's Association helpline at 800-272-3900.

faq.q: Can I take Paid Family Leave a day at a time?
faq.a: Yes. PFL can be taken in full-day increments instead of all at once. The number of days depends on how many days a week you usually work, so a three-day-a-week worker can take up to 36 days.

faq.q: Does New York have a tax credit for family caregivers?
faq.a: There is no general caregiver credit. The state child and dependent care credit can cover care for a disabled spouse or adult dependent who lived with you more than half the year. The long-term care insurance credit is 20% of qualifying premiums, up to $1,500.

title: Caring for an aging parent in New York: the first 90 days
seoTitle: Caring for an Aging Parent in New York: First 90 Days
seoDesc: A first 90 days plan for caring for an aging parent in New York: who to call, the health care proxy and POA, benefits to check, home safety and care options.
dek: Your mom or dad needs more help and you are not sure where to begin. Here is who to call, the papers to sign, the benefits to check and how to weigh home care against assisted living or a nursing home.
keyFacts: First call: NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 in NYC
Health care proxy needs two adult witnesses, no lawyer or notary
Power of attorney needs a notary and two witnesses; the notary can be one
Hospitals must let patients name a caregiver before discharge (CARE Act)
Medicare form CMS-10106 lets Medicare talk to you about your parent's claims
body:
When your mom or dad in New York starts needing more help, make two calls first. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 if your parent lives in one of the five boroughs. Then get a health care proxy and a power of attorney signed while your parent can still sign them.

The first three months after a fall, a diagnosis or a hospital stay can feel like a blur. This guide puts the work in order. It covers who to call, which papers matter most, the benefits worth checking, simple home safety fixes and how to tell when home care, assisted living or a nursing home makes sense.

Who should I call first when my parent needs more help?

Start with NY Connects. It is the state's free, unbiased front door for long-term services and supports, and it serves older adults and people with disabilities of any age, no matter how care is paid for. Staff can link you to home care, meals and transportation and help with benefit applications.

  • Outside New York City: call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or your parent's county Office for the Aging directly. There is a local office for the aging in every county.
  • In the five boroughs: call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC). NYC Aging is the one office for the whole city.

Call the office where your parent lives, not where you live. If you are in Albany and your dad is in Syracuse, Onondaga County is the office that can send someone to his home.

BoroughNY Connects partner listed by NYC AgingPhone
BronxNeighborhood SHOPP347-862-5200
BrooklynPSS718-671-6200
ManhattanHudson Guild212-966-9852
QueensSelfhelp Community Services718-559-4400
Staten IslandCommunity Agency for Senior Citizens718-489-3954

In the city, NYC Aging also funds local case management agencies for residents 60 and older. A case manager does a phone intake, then visits the home to check eligibility and set up services such as home-delivered meals or help applying for benefits. NYC Aging says its case managers do not charge for their time, though some services carry a fee or a suggested contribution based on income. Our NY Connects guide has more detail.

Call the county where your parent lives. That office is the one that can send help to the door.

What should I do in the first week after a hospital stay?

Ask to be named as your parent's caregiver before discharge. New York's CARE Act says hospitals must give each patient at least one chance to name a caregiver before discharge or transfer.

According to the Department of Health's Caregiver Guide, once a caregiver is named the hospital must:

  • Try to tell you before your parent is moved to another facility or sent home.
  • Talk with you and your parent about care needs at home.
  • Offer you training in the tasks you will do after discharge.
  • List you, the recommended care and community resources in the discharge plan.

Use that meeting. Ask what medicines changed, what warning signs mean a call to the doctor, who will deliver equipment and when the follow-up visit is. Write it down or ask for it in writing. If your parent is going home with skilled needs, read our guide to home care agencies before the first agency calls.

Which legal papers should be in place in the first month?

The two documents that matter most are a health care proxy and a durable power of attorney. Both have to be signed by your parent while they still have capacity, so do not wait.

DocumentWhat it doesHow it is signed in New York
Health care proxyNames a health care agent to make medical decisions if your parent cannotTwo adult witnesses. No lawyer or notary. The agent cannot be a witness.
Power of attorneyNames an agent for money matters such as banking and billsAcknowledged before a notary and witnessed by two people not named as agents. The notary may be one of the two.
MOLST (DOH-5003)Medical orders about CPR and other life-sustaining treatmentSigned by a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant after a conversation with your parent or their agent

The health care proxy does not cover money. The Attorney General's office says it gives no power over financial decisions, which is why the power of attorney matters too. Anyone 18 or older can serve as a health care agent, and your parent can name an alternate.

MOLST is meant for people with serious health conditions who live in or need long-term care, or who might die within the next year. Under state law it is the only authorized form for both a nonhospital do not resuscitate (DNR) and do not intubate (DNI) order. The signed form should travel with your parent between settings.

Give copies of the proxy to the agent, the main doctor and close family. Keep a copy where someone can reach it, not in a safe deposit box. See our guides to the health care proxy and MOLST and to power of attorney. If your parent can no longer sign, a court guardianship may be the only path, which is slower and costs more. Our Article 81 guide explains it.

Two more forms that save hours later

  • Medicare authorization. Form CMS-10106, the Authorization to Disclose Personal Health Information, lets Medicare talk to you about your parent's claims and records.
  • Social Security. If your parent can no longer manage their benefits, Social Security can appoint a representative payee. Call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) to ask about it.

What money and benefits should we check?

Do a benefits check in the first month. NY Connects and your county Office for the Aging can screen your parent for most of these at once.

  • Prescriptions: EPIC, the state drug plan, and Medicare Extra Help.
  • Medicare costs: the Medicare Savings Program can pay the Part B premium for people under its income limits.
  • Long-term care: Medicaid pays for home care and nursing home care for people who qualify.
  • Food and heat: SNAP and HEAP.
  • Housing costs: Enhanced STAR, the senior homeowners exemption and, in NYC, SCRIE for renters.

Make a simple list of income, accounts, insurance cards, the pharmacy and every doctor. That list is what a case manager will ask for. While you are looking at accounts, watch for warning signs such as unpaid bills, new names on accounts or sudden large withdrawals. If you suspect someone is taking advantage, our Adult Protective Services guide explains how to report it.

If you work for a covered New York employer, Paid Family Leave can cover time off to care for a parent, including a parent who lives out of state. It pays 67% of your average weekly wage for up to 12 weeks, up to $1,287.91 a week for leave starting in 2027. Our caregiver support guide covers it.

How do I make my parent's home safer?

Start with falls. The state Department of Health says falls are the leading cause of injury deaths, hospital stays and emergency visits for adults 65 and older, and that they are preventable.

The Health Department's tips are simple and cheap:

  • Clear stairs and walkways of anything that can trip someone.
  • Remove small rugs or tape them down with double-sided tape.
  • Put grab bars by the toilet and in the tub or shower, plus non-slip mats.
  • Keep everyday items within reach without a step stool.
  • Wear shoes or slippers with rubber soles indoors.
  • Ask the doctor to review all medicines, since some cause dizziness, and get eyes checked at least once a year.

Ask your county office about help with costs. Through EISEP, older adults who qualify may get ancillary services such as home repairs or assistive devices. The family caregiver program's supplemental services can include personal emergency response systems. See our EISEP guide.

How do we choose between home care, assisted living and a nursing home?

Match the setting to the kind of help your parent needs and how often. Ask two questions. Can your parent stay safe at home with help? Do they need nursing care around the clock?

OptionWho it fitsHow it is paid
Help at home (EISEP, home care agency, Medicaid home care)Needs help with some daily tasks but is safe at home with that helpEISEP for people 60+ not eligible for Medicaid, Medicaid, or private pay
PACE55+, needs a nursing home level of care but can live at home with helpMedicare and/or Medicaid. People without Medicaid pay a monthly premium.
Adult home, enriched housing or assisted living residenceCannot live on their own but does not need constant nursing careAsk each residence. Some adult homes and enriched housing programs run an Assisted Living Program for people medically eligible for nursing home care.
Nursing homeNeeds ongoing nursing or medical careMedicare generally does not cover long-term nursing home care. Most people start by paying out of pocket. Medicaid can pay once your parent qualifies.

The Department of Health licenses adult homes, enriched housing and assisted living residences. It says these are non-medical settings and are not licensed to give the continual nursing care a nursing home does. Some assisted living residences hold extra certification: an Enhanced Assisted Living Residence can keep residents who need hands-on help to walk, and a Special Needs Assisted Living Residence serves people with dementia.

Before you choose, read our guides to PACE, CDPAP, nursing home ratings and hospice. For residents of nursing homes and assisted living, the state Long Term Care Ombudsman Program is an advocate for residents at 1-855-582-6769.

What does a 90-day plan look like?

  1. Days 1 to 7: make the calls. Call NY Connects or Aging Connect, and ask to be named caregiver if your parent is in the hospital.
  2. Days 1 to 30: sign the papers. Health care proxy, power of attorney, Medicare authorization, and a MOLST conversation with the doctor if your parent is seriously ill.
  3. Days 7 to 30: get an assessment. Let the county office, NYC Aging case manager or home care agency visit and write a care plan.
  4. Days 15 to 45: check benefits. Apply for every program your parent may qualify for, starting with prescriptions and Medicare costs.
  5. Days 15 to 60: fix the home. Grab bars, lighting, clear paths and a medicine review.
  6. Days 30 to 90: plan for you. Set up respite, a support group or Paid Family Leave so you can keep going.
  7. Day 90: review. Is the plan working? If needs have grown, revisit the options above.

If you are helping from New Jersey or another state, read our long-distance caregiving guide. If memory loss is part of the picture, start with our dementia help guide. If you want a paid professional to coordinate everything, see what a geriatric care manager does.

faq.q: Who do I call to get help for my aging mom in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469. NYC Aging can connect your mom with a local case management agency, which does a phone intake and a home visit and can arrange meals, benefits help and, if she is not on Medicaid, city-funded home care. Brooklyn's NY Connects partner, PSS, is at 718-671-6200.

faq.q: My dad in Westchester just got out of the hospital. What do I do first?
faq.a: Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to reach the Westchester office for the aging, and make sure you were named as his caregiver so the hospital trains you on his care at home. Then confirm his follow-up visits and get a health care proxy and power of attorney signed if he does not have them.

faq.q: Does a health care proxy let me pay my parent's bills?
faq.a: No. A New York health care proxy covers medical decisions only. For banking and bills your parent needs a power of attorney, signed before a notary and two witnesses while they still have capacity.

faq.q: What is MOLST and does my parent need one?
faq.a: MOLST is New York's form for medical orders about CPR and other life-sustaining treatment. It is meant for people with serious health conditions who live in or need long-term care, or who might die within the next year. A physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant signs it after talking with your parent.

faq.q: Can I take paid time off to care for my parent?
faq.a: If you work for a covered New York employer, Paid Family Leave can pay 67% of your average weekly wage for up to 12 weeks to care for a parent with a serious health condition, even one who lives out of state. The cap is $1,287.91 a week for leave starting in 2027.

faq.q: When is it time for assisted living instead of home care?
faq.a: Consider it when your parent cannot live safely on their own even with help at home, but does not need ongoing nursing care. New York's adult homes and assisted living residences are non-medical settings. If your parent needs continual nursing care, a nursing home or PACE may fit better.

title: Dementia and Alzheimer's help for New York families
seoTitle: Dementia and Alzheimer's Help in New York
seoDesc: Where New York families get dementia help: state Alzheimer's programs, Centers of Excellence, respite, NYSOFA caregiver support, safety, legal papers and care.
dek: A parent with Alzheimer's or another dementia changes everything. Here are the state-funded programs, where they are near NYC and the Hudson Valley, and the legal, safety and care steps to take.
keyFacts: Alzheimer's Association 24-hour helpline: 800-272-3900
NY funds 10 Centers of Excellence and 10 regional caregiver support programs
Medicare Part B covers a separate cognitive assessment and care planning visit
Caregiver support covers caregivers of a person of any age with dementia
Missing vulnerable adult: call 911. State clearinghouse: 1-800-346-3543
body:
New York funds three statewide programs for families facing Alzheimer's disease or another dementia: regional Centers of Excellence for diagnosis, caregiver support programs with respite, and Alzheimer's Association chapters with a 24-hour helpline at 800-272-3900. Your county Office for the Aging, or NYC Aging in the five boroughs, adds caregiver counseling, support groups and respite on top of that.

This guide explains each program as the state describes it, who runs it near New York City and the Hudson Valley, how to get a diagnosis covered by Medicare, the legal papers to sign early, safety steps and the care options as needs grow.

What is dementia, and how does it change over time?

The state Department of Health describes dementia as a gradual, progressive decline in memory, thinking, problem solving, communication and attention that gets in the way of daily life. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, accounting for 60% to 80% of cases.

The Health Department says Alzheimer's is not a normal part of aging. Memory loss is mild early on. In the late stage, people lose the ability to carry on a conversation and complete daily tasks. People with Alzheimer's live an average of eight years after symptoms become noticeable, with a range of four to 20 years depending on age and other conditions.

That timeline is why planning early matters. The legal and money decisions are easiest while your parent can still take part.

Plan while your parent can still sit at the table and say what they want.

How do we get a diagnosis, and does Medicare pay?

Yes. Medicare Part B covers a separate visit for a full cognitive assessment. During that visit the doctor can confirm a diagnosis such as dementia or Alzheimer's, review medicines and build a care plan.

According to Medicare, the visit can include:

  • An exam, a medical history and a medication review
  • A look at your parent's supports, including care you can provide
  • A care plan for symptoms, and help with an advance care plan
  • Referrals to specialists and community resources such as adult day health programs and support groups

After the Part B deductible, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. You can come along to listen and answer questions. Medicare also covers cognitive assessments by telehealth through December 31, 2027, which helps if you live far away. Medicare says some people with dementia and their unpaid caregivers may get extra support through the GUIDE Model pilot, so ask whether your parent's provider takes part.

For a more specialized workup, the state's Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease are the regional experts in diagnosis and management. They also refer families to community support and promote research and clinical trials.

What dementia programs does New York State fund?

The Department of Health funds three initiatives. Each one has providers assigned by county.

ProgramWho runs itWhat it offers
Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's DiseaseTen regional centersDiagnosis, treatment and management, referrals to community support, research and clinical trial referrals, support for primary care doctors
Alzheimer's Disease Community Assistance ProgramSeven Alzheimer's Association chapters24-hour helpline, care planning and consultation, caregiver education, support groups
Alzheimer's Disease Regional Caregiver Support InitiativeTen regional community organizationsCaregiver assessments, support groups, education, wellness programs and respite

The Health Department says respite under the Regional Caregiver Support Initiative lets the main caregiver safely leave the person with dementia for short or longer periods, and can include overnight stays. Volunteers or paid workers provide it, based on your parent's level of function and your needs.

Who provides these programs near New York City and the Hudson Valley?

Here is what the Department of Health's county list shows for the areas closest to New Jersey. Check the full county list for any other county, since providers can change.

Where your parent livesRegional Caregiver Support InitiativeCenter of Excellence
Bronx, Brooklyn, Staten IslandPresbyterian Senior Services (PSS Circle of Care), 866-665-1713Columbia University Medical Center 212-305-2316, NYU Langone 212-263-3210 or SUNY Downstate 718-270-2003 (the Bronx also lists Montefiore)
ManhattanNYU Langone Medical Center, 646-754-2277Columbia, NYU Langone or SUNY Downstate
QueensSunnyside Community Services (Caregiver Support), 877-577-9337Columbia, NYU Langone or SUNY Downstate
Westchester, Rockland, SullivanAlzheimer's Association Hudson Valley Chapter, 845-471-2655Montefiore Health System, Center for the Aging Brain, 914-375-4880
Orange, PutnamNone listed; call NY ConnectsMontefiore Health System, 914-375-4880
Nassau, SuffolkParker Jewish Institute (Willing Hearts, Helpful Hands), 516-586-5107Stony Brook University, 631-954-2323

Where a program's own website shows a different phone number for caregivers than the state list, we show the program's number. The state lists the Alzheimer's Association's 24-hour helpline at 800-272-3900 for the Community Assistance Program in every area above except Orange and Putnam. The Alzheimer's Association Hudson Valley Chapter says it serves Orange and Putnam too, and it schedules help through the same helpline. This list is for finding help, not an endorsement. You can also check the Rockland, Westchester, Orange and Queens county pages for local offices.

What help do caregivers get from NYSOFA and NYC Aging?

The National Family Caregiver Support Program, run by county Offices for the Aging and NYC Aging, covers family caregivers of a person of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder. Your parent does not have to be 60 for you to qualify.

  • Case management to assess your needs and coordinate services.
  • Counseling, support groups and training on caregiving problems, including health and money.
  • Respite, either in the home or out of the home at an adult day program, senior center, nursing home or assisted living residence.
  • Supplemental services such as home-delivered meals, personal emergency response systems and legal services.

NYSOFA also funds Caregiver Resource Centers in 17 counties, including Westchester, Rockland, Orange, Putnam, Sullivan and Nassau. They offer training, counseling and support groups, and you do not have to live with your parent to use them.

In the five boroughs, call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and say you are a dementia caregiver. NYC Aging works with community groups for support groups, counseling, training, respite and limited financial help. It also funds some social adult day programs, which offer socialization, supervision, personal care and meals and give you set time off. Elsewhere, call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. Our caregiver support guide covers these programs in more depth.

Which legal papers should we sign right after a diagnosis?

Sign a health care proxy and a power of attorney as soon as possible. New York's power of attorney must be signed by a principal with capacity, and dementia takes that capacity away over time.

  1. Health care proxy. The Health Department lists Alzheimer's and other dementias among the situations where an agent is needed. Your parent signs with two adult witnesses. No lawyer or notary is needed. See our health care proxy and MOLST guide.
  2. Talk about wishes. Write down what matters to your parent about treatment and comfort care, so the agent can follow those wishes later.
  3. Power of attorney. Signed before a notary and two witnesses so an agent can manage money. See our power of attorney guide.
  4. Medicare and Social Security. File form CMS-10106 so Medicare can talk to you, and ask Social Security about a representative payee if your parent can no longer manage benefits.
  5. MOLST, when the time comes. As the illness advances, ask the doctor about a MOLST, the state form for medical orders about CPR and other life-sustaining treatment.
  6. If it is too late to sign. A court may need to appoint a guardian. Read our Article 81 guardianship guide.

Your county Office for the Aging can help you find legal services and advance planning help, such as health care proxies and wills, according to the state Office for the Aging.

How do we keep a parent with dementia safe?

Start with getting lost and falls. Then look at money, since memory loss makes it harder to spot a bad deal.

  • If your parent goes missing, the state advises searching the immediate area for no more than 15 minutes, then calling 911. Tell police your parent has dementia and is a vulnerable adult. The state Missing Persons Clearinghouse supports families of missing vulnerable adults and runs alerts for vulnerable adults who are missing and at risk of harm. Its hotline is 1-800-346-3543.
  • Keep a recent photo and a written description ready to give police.
  • Ask about Project Lifesaver. The state says many county sheriff's offices offer this tracking program, which uses a transmitter worn on the wrist or ankle. Ask your sheriff or police department whether your parent is eligible.
  • Cut fall risks. The Health Department's tips include clear walkways, taped-down or removed rugs, grab bars, non-slip mats, rubber-soled shoes and a medicine review, since some drugs cause dizziness.
  • Ask about a personal emergency response system, which the caregiver program can sometimes fund.
  • Watch money closely. Check bank statements and mail often. Our Adult Protective Services guide explains how to report exploitation.

What care options exist as dementia progresses?

Needs change as dementia moves through its stages. The right step depends on your parent's safety and your own health, and it is fine to revisit the choice.

  • Home care. EISEP for people 60+ not eligible for Medicaid, Medicaid home care or CDPAP, or a licensed home care agency.
  • Adult day programs. Social adult day care, or adult day health care, which Medicaid managed long-term care plans cover.
  • PACE. All-in-one care for people 55+ who need a nursing home level of care but can live at home. See our PACE guide.
  • Special Needs Assisted Living Residence. The Health Department certifies these residences to serve people with dementia or cognitive impairments under an individualized service plan.
  • Nursing home. For ongoing nursing care. Compare homes with our nursing home ratings guide.
  • Hospice. For comfort care near the end of life. See our hospice guide.

If you work for a covered New York employer, Paid Family Leave lists Alzheimer's disease as an example of a serious health condition. It can pay you 67% of your average weekly wage for up to 12 weeks, up to $1,287.91 a week for leave starting in 2027. For the wider plan, see our first 90 days guide and, if you live in another state, our long-distance caregiving guide.

faq.q: Where can I get help for my mom with dementia in the Bronx?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and say you are a dementia caregiver. The state's list shows Presbyterian Senior Services for the Regional Caregiver Support Initiative in the Bronx. Its caregiver program, PSS Circle of Care, is at 866-665-1713, and the Alzheimer's Association 24-hour helpline is 800-272-3900.

faq.q: How do I get respite for my dad with Alzheimer's in Westchester?
faq.a: Ask the Westchester office for the aging (through NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871) about caregiver respite, and call the Alzheimer's Association Hudson Valley Chapter at 845-471-2655, which the state lists for caregiver support there. State-funded dementia respite can include overnight stays.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a dementia evaluation?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare Part B covers a separate visit to review cognitive function, confirm a diagnosis such as dementia or Alzheimer's disease and make a care plan. After the Part B deductible, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount.

faq.q: What is a Center of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease?
faq.a: It is one of ten regional centers funded by the state Department of Health. They diagnose and manage Alzheimer's and related dementias, refer families to community support, support primary care doctors and refer patients to research and clinical trials.

faq.q: Can my parent with dementia still sign a power of attorney?
faq.a: Only if they still have capacity. New York requires a power of attorney to be signed by a principal with capacity, before a notary and two witnesses. If your parent can no longer sign, a court guardianship may be needed.

faq.q: What should I do if my parent with dementia wanders off?
faq.a: Search the immediate area for no more than 15 minutes, then call 911 and tell police your parent has dementia and is a vulnerable adult. The state Missing Persons Clearinghouse supports families and runs alerts for missing vulnerable adults at risk of harm. Its hotline is 1-800-346-3543.

title: EISEP in New York: home care for older adults not on Medicaid
seoTitle: EISEP in New York: Who Qualifies and How to Apply
seoDesc: EISEP pays for home care for New Yorkers 60+ who are not on Medicaid. Who qualifies, the cost share, services, waiting lists and how to apply in NYC and beyond.
dek: The Expanded In-home Services for the Elderly Program helps New Yorkers 60 and older who need help at home but do not qualify for Medicaid. Here is who gets it, what it costs and how to apply.
keyFacts: For New Yorkers 60+ who need help with 1 daily activity or 2 household tasks
Not for people eligible for the same services through Medicaid
No cost share at or below 150% of the federal poverty level
Full cost at or above 250% of poverty, sliding scale in between
Apply through your county Office for the Aging, NY Connects (1-800-342-9871) or Aging Connect (212-244-6469)
body:
EISEP pays for help at home for New Yorkers 60 and older who need a hand with daily tasks but are not on Medicaid. You apply through your county Office for the Aging, or through NYC Aging if you live in the five boroughs.

The full name is the Expanded In-home Services for the Elderly Program. It began in 1987. It fills the gap for older adults who have too much income or savings for Medicaid but cannot easily pay a home care agency's full rate. This guide covers who qualifies, what it pays for, the cost share and how to get on the list.

What is EISEP?

EISEP is a state program run locally by Area Agencies on Aging. Outside New York City, that means your county Office for the Aging. In the city, NYC Aging runs it through community case management agencies.

Every EISEP client gets a trained case manager. That person visits, assesses what help is needed, sets up services and checks in over time. The case manager can also connect you to other help, such as home-delivered meals or benefits screening.

EISEP is not an entitlement. It runs on a yearly state budget amount plus federal and local money, and each local Area Agency on Aging must put in a 25% local match. When the money for the year is committed, new clients may wait.

EISEP is for the parent who is too comfortable for Medicaid and too strapped for full-price home care.

The state Office for the Aging testified to the State Assembly in October 2024. It said 10,585 people were getting personal care through these programs from all funding sources. The average client was 82 to 83 years old.

Who qualifies for EISEP?

RequirementRule
Age60 or older
NeedHelp with at least one activity of daily living (such as bathing or dressing) or two instrumental activities (such as housekeeping, cooking or shopping)
SafetyCan be kept safely at home with the help
MedicaidNot eligible for the same services through Medicaid
IncomeNo income limit to apply, but income sets your cost share

The Medicaid rule is the one that trips families up. If your parent looks eligible for Medicaid, the county will usually steer them to Medicaid home care instead. Some counties, such as Onondaga, also say people who qualify for VA-funded home care are not eligible. In NYC, the rule is that a client cannot be eligible for aide or housekeeping services through another government program, including Medicaid or Medicare.

Examples of what counts as a need

  • Activities of daily living: bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, moving from bed to chair, eating.
  • Instrumental activities: light housekeeping, laundry, meal preparation, shopping, errands.

Say your mother in Schenectady can bathe and dress on her own, but since her hip replacement she cannot vacuum, carry laundry or shop. That is two instrumental activities, which can be enough to qualify.

What services can EISEP pay for?

  • Case management. Assessment, a care plan, follow-up and connection to other community services.
  • Personal Care Level I. Housekeeping, cooking, shopping and similar household tasks.
  • Personal Care Level II. Hands-on help with activities of daily living, such as bathing, dressing and grooming.
  • Consumer directed in-home services. In some counties, the client hires and directs their own aide. The state reported almost 1,000 people in 42 counties using this option in 2024.
  • Respite for family caregivers. A break for the caregiver that does not involve a stay in a nursing home or other facility.
  • Ancillary services. Goods and services that help someone stay home, such as minor home repairs, assistive devices or personal items.

How aides are hired varies by county. Some counties use licensed home care agencies. Others hire aides directly. The state said 14 Area Agencies on Aging had started hiring aides directly or working with one agency exclusively.

Hour limits in New York City

NYC Aging's home care standards cap service at 8 hours a week for clients who only need housekeeping, and 20 hours a week for clients who need personal care and housekeeping. The case management agency can add hours for special situations, such as an escort to a doctor's appointment. Counties outside the city set their own limits, so ask yours.

How much does EISEP cost?

Some clients pay nothing. Others pay part or all of the cost, based on income compared with the federal poverty level.

Household incomeWhat the client pays
At or below 150% of the federal poverty levelNo cost share
Between 150% and 250% of povertyA share of the cost on a sliding scale
At or above 250% of povertyThe full cost of services

In Onondaga County, for example, clients below the cost share threshold do not have to pay but may contribute if they are able. The county says about 40% of its clients fall below that line. Ask your county how it sets the sliding scale.

Your case manager will do a financial review at the first visit. Have these ready:

  • Social Security and pension award letters
  • Recent bank statements
  • Rent, mortgage, property tax and utility costs
  • Health insurance cards and a medication list

In NYC, a client who will not share financial information must agree to pay the maximum cost share. If you disagree with the cost share, a denial or a discharge, you have the right to ask for a hearing. You can ask out loud or in writing, within 30 days of getting the notice.

How do I apply for EISEP?

  1. Call the right office. Outside NYC, call your county Office for the Aging or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. In the five boroughs, call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC), Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and ask for a home care assessment.
  2. Answer the screening questions. Expect questions about age, health, what your parent can and cannot do, current help and income.
  3. Have the home visit. A case manager assesses needs, reviews finances and takes a health and social history. Be honest about the hard days, not only the good ones.
  4. Get a care plan. The case manager authorizes a number of hours a week and explains the cost share.
  5. Services begin. In NYC, city standards say the home care program should start services within five business days of getting the referral.
  6. Stay in touch. The case manager keeps in contact and reassesses over time. Onondaga, for example, asks clients to check in by phone every two months and does a home reassessment each year.

If your parent already has some home care and needs more, Aging Connect and the county office can help with that too.

What if there is a waiting list?

Waiting lists are common because funding is set each year and aides are hard to find. In NYC, if fewer hours are available than were approved, a program can start with fewer hours when that is safe. The client stays on a wait list for the rest.

While you wait:

  • Ask where your parent stands on the list and when to call back.
  • Tell the case manager right away if things get worse, such as a fall or a hospital stay. The case manager may need to reassess.
  • Ask about other help in the meantime, like home-delivered meals, a day program or caregiver respite.
  • Check Medicaid eligibility again if your parent's savings are dropping. See our Medicaid guide.
  • Look at private care. Our home care agencies guide explains licenses and what to ask.

When does Medicaid home care make more sense?

EISEP is for people who are not Medicaid eligible. If your parent qualifies for Medicaid, Medicaid home care is the route to use. In some cases it can also pay a family member through the consumer directed program. See our CDPAP guide.

For some families, a PACE program may also fit. See our PACE guide. NY Connects can compare options with you in one call.

Trust and safety at home

Any aide coming into the home should come through the county, NYC Aging's contracted agency or a licensed home care agency. Do not leave cash, checkbooks or jewelry out, and tell the case manager right away if anything feels wrong.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Assuming you earn too much. There is no income cap to apply. Higher income means a higher cost share, but case management still helps.
  • Waiting until after a crisis. Getting on a list early can mean help arrives when you need it.
  • Calling the county where you live. Call the office where your parent lives.
  • Downplaying needs at the assessment. Many older adults put on a brave face for visitors. Ask to sit in.
  • Missing the hearing deadline. If services are denied, ended or the cost share looks wrong, ask for a hearing within 30 days of the notice.

faq.q: How do I get home care for my dad in Brooklyn if he is not on Medicaid?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469. NYC Aging will refer him to a local case management agency, which assesses his needs and decides whether he qualifies for city-funded home care for people 60 and older who are not eligible for Medicaid home care.

faq.q: My mom lives in Westchester and needs help with housework. Can EISEP help?
faq.a: Possibly. EISEP covers people 60 and older who need help with at least two household tasks, like cleaning and shopping, or one personal care task. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to reach the Area Agency on Aging in Westchester County and request an assessment.

faq.q: Is there an income limit for EISEP?
faq.a: There is no income limit to apply. Income sets the cost share. People at or below 150% of the federal poverty level pay nothing, those between 150% and 250% pay on a sliding scale, and those at or above 250% pay the full cost.

faq.q: Can someone on Medicaid get EISEP?
faq.a: No. EISEP is for older adults who are not eligible for the same services through Medicaid. If your parent qualifies for Medicaid, the county will usually point you to Medicaid home care instead.

faq.q: How many hours of help does EISEP give?
faq.a: It depends on the assessment and the county. In New York City, the limit is 8 hours a week for housekeeping only, and 20 hours a week for personal care plus housekeeping, with extra hours possible for special situations.

faq.q: What can I do if EISEP denies or ends services?
faq.a: You have the right to a hearing on a denial, a disputed cost share or an involuntary discharge. Ask for it out loud or in writing within 30 days of receiving the notice.

title: Geriatric care managers in New York: what they do and cost
seoTitle: Geriatric Care Managers in New York: Cost and Credentials
seoDesc: What a geriatric care manager does in New York, who pays, licenses and ALCA certifications to check, how to verify a license and free options.
dek: A geriatric care manager can coordinate a parent's care when the family can't do it all. Here is what they do, what to check before you hire one and the free alternatives in New York.
keyFacts: Care management is not a licensed profession on the NYS Office of the Professions Title VIII list
Check the underlying license (LMSW, LCSW, RN) on the state's online lookup
ALCA Advanced Professionals hold a CMC, CCM, C-ASWCM or C-SWCM certification
ALCA says fees vary and may not be covered by insurance; get them in writing
Free option: NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or NYC Aging case management at 212-244-6469
body:
A geriatric care manager, also called an Aging Life Care Professional, is a paid specialist who assesses an older adult's needs, makes a care plan and coordinates doctors, home care and family. Expect to pay privately. The Aging Life Care Association says fees vary and may not be covered by insurance.

New York does not license care management as its own profession, so the credential to check is the person's underlying license, such as a social work or nursing license. This guide explains what care managers do, how to verify a license, which certifications mean what, the questions to ask and the free help you can try first.

What does a geriatric care manager do?

A care manager acts as a guide and advocate for families caring for an older relative. The Aging Life Care Association (ALCA), a national professional association, describes the work as assessment and monitoring, planning and problem-solving, education and advocacy, and coaching family caregivers.

ALCA groups the expertise into eight areas:

  • Health and disability. Going to doctor visits, improving communication between doctor, client and family, and setting up and monitoring services such as home health or hospice.
  • Financial. Reviewing or overseeing bill paying, and explaining federal and state benefits.
  • Housing. Helping weigh and choose a level of housing or residence.
  • Families. Helping relatives cope, solve problems and work through disagreements, including long-distance caregiving.
  • Local resources. Knowing what services exist nearby and how to get them.
  • Advocacy. Pressing for the client's wishes with doctors and other providers.
  • Legal. Referring to elder law attorneys and estate planners.
  • Crisis intervention. Helping through emergency room visits, hospital stays and rehab.

ALCA says a care manager may help when your parent has several medical issues, cannot live safely at home, or has little family support. It also points to families who are burned out, live far away, disagree about care or need help with dementia behaviors.

Hire help to run the plan, and keep the family in charge of it.

Does New York license care managers?

No, not as a separate profession. Care management is not among the professions in Title VIII of the state Education Law, the list the State Education Department's Office of the Professions oversees. That list does include social work and nursing, which is where many care managers come from.

ALCA says care managers come from fields such as counseling, gerontology, mental health, nursing, occupational therapy, physical therapy, psychology and social work. It adds that many are licensed in their state in a field such as nursing or social work. So the practical test is simple. Ask what license the person holds, then look it up.

New York licenseWhat the state requires
Licensed Master Social Worker (LMSW)Master's degree in social work and the ASWB Masters exam. Can provide clinical social work only under supervision.
Licensed Clinical Social Worker (LCSW)Master's in social work with at least 12 credits of clinical coursework, 3 years of supervised post-degree experience and the ASWB Clinical exam
Registered Professional Nurse (RN)An associate or bachelor's degree in nursing from an approved program and the NCLEX-RN exam

The Office of the Professions says social workers assess clients, identify resources, advocate for clients and provide services including counseling and case management. It says RNs monitor patients' health, coordinate care and counsel patients on health conditions. Those are the skills you want in a care manager.

How do I check a care manager's license in New York?

  1. Get the full name and license type. Ask for the name as it appears on the license and whether it is LMSW, LCSW, RN or another license.
  2. Open the state lookup. Go to the Office of the Professions license verification search. The state calls it a secure, primary source for license verification, updated daily.
  3. Search by name or license number. Pick the profession, such as social work or registered professional nursing.
  4. Read the record. Check the license and registration status shown, and ask about anything that looks out of date.
  5. Check ALCA membership if claimed. ALCA offers a member verification form. Only ALCA members may use the terms Aging Life Care Professional, Aging Life Care Manager and Aging Life Care Specialist.
  6. Ask for the agreement in writing. Get the services, fees and expenses on paper before work starts.

The state notes its database is under maintenance and search results may have issues. If something looks wrong, try again later or ask the person for a copy of their registration.

What do ALCA membership levels and certifications mean?

ALCA membership is a professional credential, not a state license. ALCA says it does not endorse individual members but serves as a resource for verifying qualifications.

ALCA levelWhat ALCA requires
Advanced ProfessionalA bachelor's, master's or Ph.D. (at least one in a related field such as nursing, social work, gerontology or psychology), two years of post-degree supervised care management experience in a paid position in the last ten years (three years for other degrees), and a current ALCA-approved certification
ProfessionalA degree, a paid position serving older adults and several years of post-degree supervised experience
AssociateA degree, or a nursing associate's or diploma, or an LPN, PTA or OTA license, plus a paid position serving older adults

ALCA recognizes four certifications from three certifying bodies:

  • CMC (Care Manager Certified) from the National Academy of Certified Care Managers
  • CCM (Certified Case Manager) from the Commission for Case Manager Certification
  • C-ASWCM (Certified Advanced Social Work Case Manager) from the National Association of Social Workers
  • C-SWCM (Certified Social Work Case Manager) from the National Association of Social Workers

ALCA notes that a certificate from a university program is different from certification by one of these bodies.

What does a care manager cost, and who pays?

Plan on paying privately. ALCA says rates vary by location and experience and may not be covered by insurance, and that fees should be given in writing before services start. Ask each practice for its fee schedule.

ALCA says billing differs by practice. Some bill weekly, some monthly and some when the work is done. Most also charge out-of-pocket expenses such as mileage, supplies and calls, and there may be added fees if outside professionals are brought in. Ask about all of these before you sign.

If your parent has long-term care insurance, check the policy or call the insurer to see what it covers. Medicare and Medicaid each offer their own forms of care coordination, covered below.

What questions should I ask before hiring one?

These come from ALCA's own list, with a few added for New York families.

  • What license do you hold, and in which state? (Then check it on the state lookup.)
  • Are you an ALCA member, at what level, and which certification do you hold?
  • How long have you done care management, and do you handle cases like ours?
  • Is there a fee for the first consultation? What do ongoing services cost?
  • How are travel time and mileage billed?
  • Are you available for emergencies, and who covers off-hours?
  • Does your company also provide home care? (If so, ask how they avoid steering you to their own services.)
  • How will you report to us, and how often?
  • How do we end the arrangement?
  • Can you give references?

If a problem comes up with a licensed professional, ALCA says you can complain to the professional licensing body. For ALCA members, ALCA has a professional conduct review process, reachable at 520-881-8008.

What free help can I try first?

New York has public case management that costs nothing for the case manager's time. Try these before paying, or alongside a private care manager.

Free or covered optionWho it helpsHow to start
NY ConnectsOlder adults and people with disabilities of any age, and their families1-800-342-9871
EISEP case managementPeople 60+ not eligible for Medicaid. Every client gets a trained case manager.County Office for the Aging
NYC Aging case managementNYC residents 60+. Case managers do not charge for their time.212-244-6469
Medicare chronic care managementPeople with 2 or more serious chronic conditions expected to last a yearAsk the doctor. 20% coinsurance after the Part B deductible.
Medicaid managed long-term careMedicaid members enrolled in a managed long-term care plan. Care management is a covered service.See our Medicaid guide

Some services set up by public case managers may carry a cost share or suggested contribution based on income. See our guides to NY Connects, EISEP, Medicaid and PACE, which includes a care team. Caregivers can also get counseling and support through our caregiver support guide.

Seniors of NY does not list, rank or recommend individual care managers in this guide. For where to start, see our first 90 days guide, our long-distance caregiving guide and, if memory loss is involved, our dementia help guide.

faq.q: How do I find a care manager for my mother in Westchester?
faq.a: ALCA has a search tool for its members by ZIP code, and you should check any license on the NYS Office of the Professions lookup. Before paying, call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to ask the Westchester office for the aging about free case management such as EISEP.

faq.q: Is there free care management for my dad in Staten Island?
faq.a: Yes. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469. NYC Aging funds local case management agencies for residents 60 and older, and its case managers do not charge for their time. Some services they arrange may have a fee or suggested contribution based on income.

faq.q: Does New York license geriatric care managers?
faq.a: Not as a separate profession. Care management is not among the licensed professions in Title VIII of the Education Law, which the Office of the Professions oversees. Many care managers hold a social work or nursing license, which you can check on the state's online lookup.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a geriatric care manager?
faq.a: ALCA says care manager fees may not be covered by insurance, so ask your parent's plan. What Medicare Part B may pay for is chronic care management by a doctor or other provider, if your parent has two or more serious chronic conditions expected to last at least a year, with 20% coinsurance after the deductible.

faq.q: What does CMC mean after a care manager's name?
faq.a: CMC stands for Care Manager Certified, a certification from the National Academy of Certified Care Managers. It is one of four certifications the Aging Life Care Association accepts for its Advanced Professional level.

faq.q: Should a care manager also sell home care?
faq.a: Some practices do both. ALCA suggests asking whether the company also provides home care. If it does, ask how it makes sure its recommendations fit your parent's needs and not its own services.
